title: Your Gut May Affect Your Response to Stress — Study
paragraphs: The trillions of bacteria that live in our digestive system, known as the gut microbiome, are known to play an important role in our health. Now, a new study from Austria suggests that these bacteria may also be linked to the way our bodies respond to stress.

The study was carried out by researchers at the University of Vienna and published in the journal Neurobiology of Stress in 2026. According to reports, it involved 74 healthy adults. Some of the participants took part in a standard stress test, while others completed a similar task that was not stressful. The researchers measured the participants' levels of cortisol, a hormone that the body releases in response to stress, using samples of their saliva. They also asked the participants how stressed they felt. In addition, they analyzed samples of the participants' stool to study the bacteria in their guts.

Many people might expect that a more diverse gut microbiome would help people stay calm under pressure. However, the results were surprising. The researchers found that people with a greater variety of gut bacteria actually showed a stronger stress response, both in their cortisol levels and in how stressed they said they felt.

The researchers also looked at substances called short-chain fatty acids, which gut bacteria produce when they break down fiber. They found that a greater ability to produce one of these substances, butyrate, was linked to a stronger stress response. On the other hand, a greater ability to produce another substance, propionate, was linked to a weaker stress response.

Importantly, the researchers do not believe that a stronger stress response is necessarily a bad thing. Instead, they suggest that it may be a short-term, healthy way for the body to prepare itself to deal with a challenge.

However, the study only shows a link between gut bacteria and stress. It does not prove that the bacteria cause the differences. Experts say that long-term studies will be needed to find out whether changing the gut microbiome, for example through diet, can reliably change the way people respond to stress.
Other recent research has also suggested connections between gut bacteria and the body's stress system, though much of this work has been carried out on animals.
